tagline: A clean Double Diamond sample: from clinic phone-queue problem to tested assisted check-in pilot.

project.title: Clinic QuickCheck — assisted pre-visit check-in
project.goal: How might we reduce appointment-prep phone calls at a neighborhood clinic without excluding patients who need human help?
project.description: A simple end-to-end Double Diamond study. The team explores why the phone queue spikes, defines the real bottleneck, compares solution directions, tests an assisted pre-check-in prototype with patients and staff, and closes with a pilot decision. (Example project shipped with Sonaloop — reload or remove it any time: `sonaloop load-example onboarding-showcase` / `remove-example`.)

councils.prompt: Where does appointment preparation break down before patients arrive?
councils.selection_reason: Sponsor, daily operator, less-digital patient, and high-convenience patient cover the full workflow.
councils.summary: The phone queue is not caused by lack of reminders; it is caused by uncertainty about forms, legitimacy, and fallback.
councils.exec_summary: The discovery round reframes the problem from “move forms online” to “let patients prepare early while the clinic can see who still needs human help.”

statements.text: The calls cluster around “do I need to bring this?” and “did you get my form?” If the desk cannot see status, online prep just moves confusion upstream.
A patient-only link is not enough. I need a morning queue that says ready, missing, or needs help without opening three systems.
I would try the text if it said I can ignore it and still call. The scary part is feeling I have chosen the wrong door.
I do not need a portal. I need three minutes on my phone and a clear “you are ready” before I load the kids into the car.

councils.prompt: Choose the better pilot direction: patient-only pre-check-in or assisted pre-check-in with a staff queue.

options.label: A
options.title: Patient-only pre-check-in
options.text: Patients receive a text link, fill forms, upload insurance, and arrive ready. Staff see completion only after the EHR sync.

options.label: B
options.title: Assisted pre-check-in
options.text: Patients receive the same link, but every screen shows a call fallback and the front desk sees ready / missing / needs help before the visit.

councils.selection_reason: The Define synthesis narrowed the problem to assisted preparation; this comparison tests whether the staff queue is essential or extra.

preferences.reason: The staff queue makes the pilot measurable and reversible. Patient-only prep hides the work until it fails.
If I cannot see who needs help, I still answer the calls. B is the first version that changes my morning.
The call option is what makes the text safe. Without it I would wait and phone anyway.
I personally want the fastest path, but I understand why the clinic needs B for everyone.

statements.text: A may look simpler, but it gives me no operational control on day one.
B is pilotable because it protects both sides: patient autonomy and staff visibility.
A is another invisible inbox. I will learn about failures when the patient is already at the counter.
B gives me a morning worklist. That is the difference between a tool and a wish.
A feels like the clinic is sending me away to pass a test.
B is acceptable if the phone number is visible and the text is large enough.
A is enough for me personally; I would finish it in the pickup line.
B is fine as long as the extra safety does not slow down the fast path.

councils.exec_summary: Assisted pre-check-in wins 3–1. The staff queue is not administrative polish; it is the operational mechanism that turns patient preparation into fewer calls.
councils.summary: Head-to-head comparison of two solution directions. B wins because it keeps the human fallback visible and gives staff a pre-visit worklist.

councils.prompt: Attack the assisted pre-check-in pilot: why would it fail in the first two weeks?
councils.selection_reason: Same panel, adversarial lens after prototype sessions; the pilot should fail here before it fails with real patients.

objections.text: If the ready state does not match the EHR schedule, I will trust the EHR and ignore QuickCheck. Then the pilot becomes a second board to reconcile.
If the phone number disappears after the first screen, I will assume I am stuck and call anyway.
If we turn this on for every visit type, staff will blame the pilot for every intake problem we already had.
If the insurance upload turns into a scavenger hunt, I will abandon and arrive early like before.

statements.text: The whole pilot lives or dies on whether the staff queue is more trustworthy than a sticky note.
Do not make the fallback a footnote. It has to be part of the product.
Keep the pilot to annual physicals and medication follow-ups. That is narrow enough to learn.

councils.exec_summary: The red team does not kill the concept. It narrows the launch: two appointment types, visible call fallback on every screen, and a staff queue reconciled before opening hours.
councils.summary: Objection review over the proposed pilot. The main blockers become explicit pilot requirements.

hypotheses.text: If the prototype keeps a visible call fallback and a staff-ready queue, at least 75% of tested users will complete appointment prep without saying they would call the clinic.

sections.heading: What discovery changed
sections.markdown:
The first discovery council showed that appointment-prep calls are not mainly reminder calls. They are uncertainty calls: patients ask whether forms arrived, whether insurance is missing, what they should bring, and whether calling is still safer than using a portal.

:::insight
The root problem is not awareness of the appointment. It is confidence that preparation is complete and recoverable if something goes wrong.
:::

citations.quote: Most calls ask whether prep was received or what to bring.

sections.heading: Point of view
sections.markdown:
The clinic should not prototype pure self-service. The better direction is assisted preparation: a short patient path that says exactly what is done, plus a staff queue that makes missing prep visible before the patient arrives.

:::recommendation
Prototype the patient and staff sides together. If staff cannot see readiness states, the prototype cannot honestly test whether calls go down.
:::

citations.quote: I need a morning queue that says ready, missing, or needs help.

syntheses.title: Deliver synthesis — assisted check-in pilot
syntheses.start_input: Synthesize option comparison, prototype sessions, and red-team objections into a launchable pilot.
syntheses.goal: Conclude the Double Diamond with a buildable pilot spec.

payload.arc_narrative: The solution diamond converged on assisted pre-check-in: not pure self-service, not a lobby kiosk, but a short SMS path paired with a staff queue.
payload.gesamtbild: Pilot readiness depends on three must-haves: visible call fallback on every patient screen, ready/missing/needs-help states for staff, and a narrow launch scope.
payload.positionierung: QuickCheck is a pre-visit preparation loop for clinics that want fewer calls without abandoning patients who need help.

findings.text: Assisted pre-check-in beat patient-only self-service because staff visibility is required to reduce calls.
Prototype sessions validated the short flow, but only with a visible fallback and an EHR match indicator.
The pilot should start with annual physicals and medication follow-ups, not all appointment types.

citations.quote: Keep the pilot to annual physicals and medication follow-ups.

statements.text: This is narrow enough to run and concrete enough to stop if it creates desk work.
I would pilot it if ready/missing/needs-help matches the schedule before opening.
I can use it if calling remains a first-class option.

syntheses.lead: The solution diamond closed on QuickCheck: an optional SMS pre-check-in flow paired with a staff readiness queue, piloted narrowly before clinic-wide rollout.

sections.heading: Chosen concept
sections.markdown:
The head-to-head comparison rejected a patient-only check-in flow. That option was faster on paper, but it did not give staff the operational visibility needed to reduce calls. The selected concept is assisted pre-check-in: patients complete a three-step flow, while staff see ready, missing, and needs-help states before the desk opens.

:::key
QuickCheck is not a portal replacement. It is a preparation loop between patient and front desk.
:::

citations.quote: If it does not change my morning queue, it will not change call volume.

sections.heading: Prototype evidence
sections.markdown:
Three prototype sessions validated the direction, with important constraints. Luis completed the staff-view scenario but wanted an EHR match indicator before trusting the queue. Evelyn completed the patient flow only because the call option stayed visible. Priya completed quickly and wanted the confirmation state to say exactly what changed at arrival.

:::insight
The prototype works when digital completion and human recovery are visible at the same time. Hiding either one turns the experience back into uncertainty.
:::

citations.quote: Completed the staff queue, but asked for an EHR match indicator.
Completed only after seeing the call option remain available.

sections.heading: Launch guardrails
sections.markdown:
The red team surfaced three launch risks: excluding patients who do not trust links, creating new desk work, and overextending the pilot across appointment types. The pilot should start with annual physicals and medication follow-ups, keep phone fallback visible, and review readiness-state accuracy daily.

:::risk
Do not launch clinic-wide until the staff queue proves it reduces uncertainty instead of creating a second inbox.
:::

citations.quote: Keep the pilot to annual physicals and medication follow-ups.

sections.heading: Decision
sections.markdown:
Run a four-week capped pilot with two appointment categories, one practice manager owner, daily front-desk review, and explicit stop criteria if call volume or desk work rises. Success means preparation completion improves while patients still understand how to get human help.

:::recommendation
Use the pilot as an operational test, not a conversion test. The product wins only if both patients and staff are more certain before arrival.
:::
